articles.title: Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
articles.snippet: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
articles.full_text:
Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
- Published
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described today's incidents as "malicious hoax threats".
In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".
"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".
A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.
Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.
Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
These incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.
Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".
Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".

articles.title: Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
articles.snippet: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel dies aged 30 after an on-field collision during a Spanish second-division match.
articles.full_text:
Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
- Published
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.
Reuters reported on Tuesday that police in Spain have opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true" Tenerife said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
'There are no words'
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Tenerife's president, Felipe Minambres, says the club's players will need "professional assistance" to help deal with the ordeal of one of their team-mates dying.
"We are all feeling vulnerable and deeply saddened right now. It's hard to even believe what has happened," said Minambres.
"We know, especially the players and the players' partners, that we will need support. We've already begun receiving offers of help today, and that support will continue.
"We will need professional assistance, but we also need the support of all our fans, because they are likely feeling the same way we are today."
Minambres added it had been a "truly unbelievable situation" and "an enormous tragedy that we have had to endure".
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, issued a statement later on Tuesday which spoke of the club's shock and expressed condolences to De Miguel's family, club "and all those who were close to him".
"We are deeply affected by what has happened and we share the pain that the club is experiencing," it continued.
"From the very beginning we have maintained contact with them and we are at their disposal for anything they may need.
"What has happened has had a huge emotional impact on our players, the coaching staff and everyone at FC Andorra. These are particularly difficult times for everyone and we want to make sure that no one has to face them alone. That is why the club is providing psychological support to anyone who needs it."
Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."
De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.
"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."
Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.
"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."
Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."
Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.
Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.
A lower-league player with an eye for goal
De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.
After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.
He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.
The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.
De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

articles.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
articles.snippet: An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.
articles.full_text:
Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
- Published
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".
It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.
Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.
North Korea involvement
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."
As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

articles.title: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
articles.snippet: At least 38 people are killed in 24 hours and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky warns dozens more could be trapped under rubble.
articles.full_text:
Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
- Published
Russian strikes on Ukraine â including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital â have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others across Ukraine over the last 24 hours.
At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.
He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".
Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.
The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.
Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.
Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof collapsed, trapping many underneath.
"The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen.
However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.
The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment.
According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital.
But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law", external.
Further north, in Dnipro, nearly 50 terminally ill patients were being transferred to other facilities after their hospice was destroyed by a Russian missile on Monday night. The oldest of the patients was 90 years old.
Mayor Boris Filatov posted photos on Telegram showing elderly people lying in their beds in a hospice room with blown-out windows and rubble and broken glass strewn on the floors.
"I realise that I am violating ethics," wrote Filatov. "I want as many people as possible to see these photos. Especially politicians and diplomats. Especially abroad.
"These are elderly, terminally ill people. This is a Russian missile."
Elsewhere in Dnipro, a separate strike killed two people and left 18 others wounded. Another five people were killed in aerial bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.
Russia has also struck energy infrastructure in nine regions, affecting water and heating.
The water supply in Kyiv was entirely cut off "due to enemy attacks and damage to the capital's energy infrastructure", the main water supplier Kyivvodokanal said. The entire metro network was suspended on Tuesday and Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the situation surrounding the city's power supply was becoming "very difficult".
As Ukraine was counting its dead, the Kremlin announced it would take part in three-way peace talks with Ukraine brokered by the US in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November.
It will be the first trilateral meeting since February. Since then, Russia and the US have begun engaging more directly, with US President Donald Trump announcing a deal to import Russian diesel.
Speaking to reporters in Berlin on Tuesday, Zelensky said that it was important for Russia to engage seriously in negotiations on a ceasefire and a peaceful settlement, but that he had so far had not seen "any indication" of that being the case.
Several rounds of ceasefire talks late last year yielded no results, and in public declarations Russian officials have generally refused to budge from Moscow's maximalist demand of effective Ukrainian surrender.
US First Lady Melania Trump Melania Trump, who was credited with brokering a truce last week in the besieged town of Oleshky, is set to host representatives of Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday. However, no details were given in the White House statement of who was due to attend the meeting., external
The UN said last month that civilian casualties in Ukraine had reached a "record level", as Russian armed forces resumed systematic attacks on energy infrastructure.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its advances on the front line have since stalled, and attacks on Ukraine have intensified, with Moscow employing large numbers of missiles and drones to strike Ukrainian cities.
At the same time, Ukraine is faces a critical air defense shortage due to stalled Western deliveries of weapons and a lack of American Patriot interceptor missiles.
In Berlin, Zelensky acknowledged that although the front line was stable "the situation in the air was not as positive, particularly when it comes to our air defence capabilities and the protection of our civilian population".

articles.title: Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
articles.snippet: The US company was named after the Greek goddess of victory, so the Dar al-Ifta said displaying its logo was unIslamic.
articles.full_text:
Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
- Published
Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.
It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.
The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.
Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

articles.title: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.snippet: Supermarkets have reported problems from Estonia and Sweden to Portugal and Italy and many retainers have been forced to discard food.
articles.full_text:
Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
- Published
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
- Published5 hours ago
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe BÃ¼sken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven IntermarchÃ© stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

articles.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
articles.snippet: US officials described the attacks on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
articles.full_text:
US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
- Published
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.
There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".
Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.
On Tuesday, Iran's chief negotiator with the US, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated: "The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."
"Just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.
It was not immediately clear what Ghalibaf was referring to, but Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Irna on Monday that "very intensive" talks to try to end the war were under way with the US via Qatari and Pakistani mediators.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process... We are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," Majed al-Ansari told reporters in Doha.
Last week, Iranian negotiators discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. They reportedly include lifting a naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.

articles.title: South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Shrimpers worry about fuel costs, tariffs and Trump's proposed cuts to the agency that provides vital weather data.
articles.full_text:
South Carolina shrimpers weigh costs, vote in crucial US midterms
Shrimpers worry about fuel costs, tariffs and Trump’s proposed cuts to the agency that provides vital weather data.
Mount Pleasant, South Carolina – For Mark Marhefka, the weather can be the difference between a profitable fishing trip and a dangerous one.
As a shrimper and fisherman for 49 years, Marhefka relies on forecasts, weather buoys and data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to decide when it is safe to take his boats offshore. With storms and warm water temperatures disrupting this year’s fishing season, he worries that President Donald Trump’s proposed funding cuts could further reduce the services fishermen depend on.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3China to suspend imports of Japanese seafood amid diplomatic row: Reports
- list 2 of 3Trump administration aims to cut regulations on US commercial fishing
- list 3 of 3Lobster industry caught in Maine’s political headwinds before US midterms
“They’ve already started cutting back on NOAA, and they’re looking to do more in this next fiscal year,” Marhefka, who owns Abundant Seafood, told Al Jazeera. “It’s definitely something that we need to fight against.”
Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, NOAA has lost roughly 20 percent of its workforce, according to an analysis of federal employment data. The administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut funding for ocean monitoring and terminate a programme supporting regional ocean observations.
But the weather is only one of the pressures facing South Carolina shrimpers as they head to the polls on Tuesday for the US midterm elections.
Rising fuel prices, equipment costs and competition from imported shrimp are weighing on people who make their living from the water.
Marhefka believes Democrats could address these pressures better than Republicans.
“Fuel costs have doubled since Trump has been back in office,” said Marhefka. “I voted Democrat because I really think Annie Andrews is going to help South Carolina.”
At an election-eve rally in Charleston on Monday, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, Annie Andrews, sought to appeal to voters like Marhefka, arguing that her campaign would address the financial pressures facing coastal communities.
“I’m fighting for a South Carolina that we can afford,” Andrews said to the crowd. “I’m fighting to lower the damn diesel for our farmers and our fishermen and our shrimpers.”
Although shrimpers make up a small share of South Carolina’s electorate, their concerns raise bigger questions about the cost of doing business and retirement planning.
John Henry Middleton, an 81-year-old fisherman who has been shrimping for about 50 years, is an undecided voter. He says he is frustrated with both parties, arguing that politicians make promises but fail to work together on issues affecting common people.
“I want to see them get together and work for the good of the people,” he told Al Jazeera.
His concerns as he heads to the ballot box on Tuesday include the cost of living and whether he will have enough money to support himself in retirement. He said he has paid taxes and worked for decades, but still has to work at 81.
Kevin S, who declined to give his last name, works at Geechee Seafood on Shem Creek and said he plans to vote Republican on Tuesday. He said many people in the fishing industry lean Republican because they see government regulation as an obstacle to making a living.
“It’s a pretty regulated industry. A lot of red tape, a lot of extreme permits,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that some fishing permits can cost thousands of dollars.
Kevin added that rising fuel prices have increased the cost of running his business, but he doesn’t closely follow the factors driving those increases.
When asked whether the war in Iran was contributing to higher prices, he said he didn’t know enough about the issue to say. Instead, he pointed to Trump’s efforts to increase domestic energy production as a reason he thinks Republicans are better placed to address fuel costs.
He also believes many blue-collar workers share this view, but emphasised that industry support for Republicans does not necessarily mean enthusiasm for the party.
“I just don’t really trust Democrats as much to make the best financial decisions,” he said. “It’s not that a lot of people love the Republican Party. It’s more of a lesser of two evils.”
‘Not lavish living’
The pressures facing shrimpers are also evident in the dwindling number of businesses around Shem Creek, a historic fishing area near Charleston. Cindy and Taylor Tarvin, co-owners of Tarvin Seafood, estimate that only about eight shrimpers remain in the area. They say the decline reflects how difficult it has become to make a living in the industry.
“Younger captains can make a living, but not a lavish one,” Cindy Tarvin told Al Jazeera.
The Tarvins said their diesel costs rose sharply this year. They started the year paying $2.71 per gallon (3.78 litres), but by late September they were paying $5.99 per gallon. The American Automobile Association (AAA) reported that South Carolina’s average retail diesel price reached a record $6.17 that month.
Maintenance and equipment costs have also risen, adding to the financial strain on boat owners.
“There will always be a demand for watermen and what they produce. What scale they’re able to do it at is the big question,” Taylor Tarvin told Al Jazeera.
The Tarvins agree that one of the biggest challenges is the volume of imported shrimp entering the US market. Shrimp from abroad is often sold at lower prices, making it difficult for domestic fishermen to compete.
They said the influx of imports has contributed to falling prices and razor-thin profit margins, forcing some local boats out of business.
The competition extends well beyond South Carolina. According to the Southern Shrimp Alliance, the United States imported 1.59 billion pounds, or about 721,000 tonnes, of frozen warmwater shrimp in 2025, a 2 percent increase from the previous year.
In July 2026, the Trump administration imposed additional tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on imported shrimp from major suppliers including India, Ecuador, Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand.
Trump’s tariffs on imported shrimp initially raised hopes among domestic shrimpers that foreign products would become more expensive and local catch more competitive. But the Tarvins said they have yet to see a meaningful benefit in the prices they receive, and are unsure whether they ever will.
There is another complication. Tariffs on imported steel, aluminium and products made from those materials have increased the cost of maintaining boats.
“So all of the pieces and parts that go into keeping a fishing boat running and keeping the equipment replaceable are affected by tariffs,” Cindy said.
For Marhefka, rising costs are part of a broader frustration with the country’s direction. He says he tries not to discuss politics often, but has heard growing frustration from those who voted for Trump and feel their circumstances have worsened.
“I just don’t think that we can go and handle another two more years of this,” he said. “We’re just getting squeezed too hard.”

articles.title: Darfur survivors vow to tell story of those killed after Sudan camp attacks
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and violence that forced them to flee.
articles.full_text:
Darfur survivors vow to tell story of those killed after Sudan camp attacks
Survivors of attacks on displacement camps in Darfur recall the lives they built, and the violence that forced them to flee.
In a small house in Omdurman, Hassan Saber Jumaa, a senior administrator at the Zamzam displacement camp in Sudan, sat on a simple wooden chair. He scrolled through his phone, looking for any photograph he might have of Zamzam, which is near el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, and once sheltered hundreds of thousands.
He found nothing. Jumaa explained that his old phone was looted during last year’s attack by Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces on the camp. Pointing to the bare walls around him, Jumaa said that all he has left are his memories of the camp, and the people who once called it home.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3Sudan’s displaced return to new challenges in war-battered Khartoum
- list 3 of 3Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power system
Zamzam, established in 2004, was home to generations of people displaced by western Sudan’s Darfur war, which began in 2003 and continued for nearly two decades. Alongside Abu Shouk camp and al-Salam camp, Zamzam formed part of one of Darfur’s largest concentrations of displaced people.
Jumaa recalled a bustling community, with its market open every day, and children walking to school.
Zamzam memories
Zamzam continued as a refuge for civilians until Sudan’s current war, which began in 2023. The RSF, fighting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its allies, captured the camp in April 2025, after months of attacks. Famine had been confirmed in the camp in August 2024.
Mukhtar Musa, a survivor of the assault, watched the community he knew descend into starvation and violence. He said restrictions on the movement of goods had exhausted food supplies, leaving some residents with little choice but to eat animal feed and peanut shells.
Umm Kulthum Ali Saleh described the months before the final attack as the hardest of her life. The RSF siege on Zamzam stopped goods from entering. She searched for food every morning, and recalled seeing women cooking grass and mixing mud with flour to bake bread.
Saleh believes the blockade was not merely a military measure, but a deliberate way to weaken the camp’s residents in advance of the final offensive, and Zamzam’s fall.
Brutal military offensive
On April 11, the RSF launched a three-day assault using cars, camels, and horses, burning straw homes and health facilities.
A United Nations Human Rights Office report documented at least 1,013 civilians killed, including 319 who were summarily executed in homes, markets, schools, clinics, and mosques. The report documented other abuses, including rape, gang rape, sexual slavery, and other forms of sexual violence, particularly targeting the Zaghawa community.
Musa was a witness to some of those mass killings, and said he saw RSF fighters kill civilians while chanting religious slogans. He described seeing bodies scattered around the main market and near schools, and said fighters continued pursuing civilians along roads leading out of the camp.
Saleh also recalled seeing bodies littering the roads, with only chickens, donkeys, and sheep wandering among the abandoned buildings.
The attack forced tens of thousands to flee Zamzam, with many remaining in the el-Fasher area, and others fleeing south to Tawila and Dar al-Salam.
The violence continued to engulf el-Fasher and its surrounding displacement camps over the following months.
With Zamzam under its control, the RSF launched an attack on el-Fasher in August 2025, and soon captured the Abu Shouk camp.
The UN Human Rights Office said at least 40 displaced people were killed inside Abu Shouk, while 19 others were injured. The International Organization for Migration reported that at least 500 residents fled the camp that day.
The RSF captured el-Fasher itself on October 26, 2025. More than 6,000 people are believed to have been killed in the attack, in el-Fasher as well as on escape routes out of the city. The UN found that RSF fighters targeted civilians, including members of non-Arab communities, and committed acts amounting to war crimes.
The RSF has previously denied targeting civilians in Zamzam and el-Fasher, while acknowledging that some fighters committed abuses.
The survivors of Zamzam, al-Shouk, and el-Fasher focus on bearing witness to the tragedy they faced.
Jumaa said the destruction of Zamzam marked not the end of the violence, but the beginning of another wave of displacement.
For him, the camp survives in the memories of those who once lived there – even as they are now displaced elsewhere.
Musa, meanwhile, said he cannot forget the first days of the siege, and the bodies he saw on the streets.
“Whoever survives must tell the story of what happened,” Musa said.

articles.title: Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: With neither bloc near a majority, Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties hold the key to Israel’s next government..
articles.full_text:
Israel political deadlock leaves Netanyahu’s future hanging in the balance
With neither bloc near a majority, Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties hold the key to Israel’s next government.
Israel’s election results are due to be certified on Wednesday, but with both leading blocs falling short of a parliamentary majority, negotiations remain deadlocked.
As things stand, the right-wing coalition of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured 53 seats in the October 27 vote, while the self-styled Zionist opposition alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot had 48. A majority requires 61 seats in the 120-strong Knesset. The 19 remaining seats went to the two Arab-led lists – the Joint List and Ra’am, or the United Arab List.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
- list 2 of 4Israeli officials say results stand as Netanyahu claims election ‘stolen’
- list 3 of 4The future of the Palestinian vote in Israel
- list 4 of 4Arab parties back Eisenkot: What’s the latest in Israel’s coalition talks?
Netanyahu’s camp has been accused of seeking to delegitimise the results after launching a series of largely discounted claims that the vote for the Arab parties, which scored their best-ever electoral performance, had been manipulated by foreign interference.
Despite their historic showing that was boosted by an unprecedented surge in voter turnout, the two Arab-led lists remain politically isolated. And while there have been indications that they would be prepared to support, or at least not oppose, an Eisenkot-led government, their backing remains contentious within the opposition – a broad and increasingly fractious alliance that also includes parties led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, left-winger Yair Golan and right-winger Avigdor Lieberman.
After a meeting on Tuesday, the main opposition leaders issued a statement announcing that they were preparing to “act immediately” to replace Netanyahu’s governing coalition “with a national emergency government and translate the clear parliamentary majority in the Knesset into action”. Yet, the statement did not specify how they would reach the majority that would ultimately depend on them allying with either the Arab-led lists or two ultra-Orthodox parties, which have historically supported Netanyahu in return for shielding some of their members from military service.
“Essentially, we’re both on track to a government, and nowhere near being able to form one,” Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak told Al Jazeera.
‘Not clear who’s talking to who’
Though informal negotiations are widely reported to have begun, official talks on establishing a governing coalition will start only after the results are certified on Wednesday. Netanyahu’s Likud party has already mooted refusing to recognise the results, citing its continuing claims of irregularities in the Arab vote. Those allegations have been investigated and discounted by police, while a separate probe by the internal security service, the Shin Bet, remains ongoing.
Once the results are certified, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with all the parties to determine which member of the Knesset, not necessarily a party leader, is best placed to form a government.
Herzog, who lost to Netanyahu after an especially bitter contest in 2015, has found himself in the unusual position of having to decide who should be given the first opportunity to form a government, while simultaneously considering the prime minister’s longstanding request for a pardon in his ongoing corruption trial.
One of Herzog’s options is to ask the Arab parties to recommend Eisenkot. If selected, the leader of the centrist Yashar party will initially have 28 days to assemble a coalition, a period that can be extended by 14 days. Should he fail, Herzog can then invite another candidate to try.
For his part, Netanyahu on Monday argued that Likud’s first-place finish, with 27 seats, gave him a mandate to lead the next government. “We aim to form a broad government with our partners and with any other party that wishes to join, provided they do not support terrorism,” he said.
Still, it is unlikely he will be able to command a majority without entering an alliance with the Arab parties that he has consistently vilified, or a large-scale wave of defections from the opposition.
Whatever the state of the negotiations, the new Knesset is due to be sworn in on November 10.
Barak said coordination within the opposition appeared minimal, while personal animosities between Netanyahu and Herzog further complicated already fraught negotiations.
“It’s really not clear who’s talking to who,” he added.
“Earlier this week, they named [Bennett’s running mate] Lapid as their choice of speaker, which was apparently news to both Eisenkot and Bennett. Equally, Netanyahu now has to appeal to his political rival, Herzog, both to be given the responsibility of forming a government and to be pardoned before any conviction,” Barak continued.
“All the while, he’s claiming that the Arab parties cannot be considered legitimate partners in government, which makes it almost impossible for anyone to form a coalition with them.”
Clear as mud
However, the extent to which the efforts to delegitimise the Arab parties may succeed remains uncertain. Ra’am served as a central plank of the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021–22, the first time an independent Arab party had formally joined an Israeli government, with public pressure to do so again growing.
Over the weekend, thousands rallied in Tel Aviv calling upon Eisenkot to make a deal with the Arab parties that reflected the overwhelming number of votes cast against Netanyahu’s governing coalition. However, following the meeting between the opposition leaders on Tuesday, sources within the Joint List told Al Jazeera they were not expecting to be invited to support the bloc anytime soon.
Instead, speculation has turned to the possibility of one of the two ultra-Orthodox parties – Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ), and particularly the latter – defecting to the opposition and backing Eisenkot.
Neither Shas nor UTJ have had straightforward relationships with Netanyahu’s governing coalition. In fact, it was the withdrawal of their parliamentary support in May, following what they saw as the coalition’s failure to pass a draft law exempting some of their ultra-Orthodox members from military service, that fundamentally weakened its majority in parliament.
“There are rumours that the Ashkenazi [Jews, who make up the bulk of the UTJ membership] are ready to break with Netanyahu and go to Eisenkot,” political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera.
“I am sceptical, but even that would still leave them short of an overall majority, so they would still need support from one of the Arab parties, even if that is Ra’am supporting them from outside a formal coalition,” he said of the parliamentary arithmetic.
Spoilers
Hanging over all, however, are developments tied to Israel’s deep and longstanding alliance with the United States.
Barak said the entire government-formation process risked being disrupted by the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, which could weaken Israel’s foremost ally, President Donald Trump, or be overtaken entirely by renewed war with Iran.
Netanyahu, particularly, went to pains during the election campaign to stress his relationship with Trump, whose Republican Party faces a tough race to keep hold of Congress.
Equally, both Trump’s rhetoric as well as the renewed build-up of US forces in the region may all signal the beginning of renewed conflict with Israel’s regional nemesis, Iran.
“Netanyahu cannot form a coalition,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera. “It’s a numbers game, and he just doesn’t have the numbers – no amount of talking and planning can change that, but an emergency could, and in Israel, there’s no more popular an emergency than one involving Iran.”
In such an instance, he speculated that the incumbent could ask the opposition to fall in behind him, but that would raise the possibility of a former captain dictating war policy to former generals.
“There’s also the possibility that, however you want to define it, Israel has a successful war against Iran. That leads to a surge in popularity for Netanyahu when negotiations on a coalition resume, or [him] calling unnecessary, fresh elections,” said Mekelberg.

Senior police spokesman Robert Netshiunda said on Tuesday that a murder investigation had been opened after Lastborn Shazi – identified by the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) – was shot dead late on Monday at his home while on a Zoom call coordinating the party’s election campaign.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
