articles.full_text:
Ukraine’s Zelenskyy hopes Abu Dhabi talks will open path to Putin meeting
Ukrainian president meets Germany’s Merz in Berlin as chancellor says Russia is yet to engage seriously in peace efforts.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he hopes upcoming United States-mediated talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi will lead to a three-way meeting of leaders that includes Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking in Berlin on Tuesday alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Zelenskyy said the adviser-level talks, set for November 10 and 11 , were part of a broader diplomatic push to end the war.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Russia detains minor over alleged Moscow attack plot after US warning
- list 2 of 3Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends
- list 3 of 3Russian attack on Ukraine aid hub kills 31 as US announces new peace talks
“We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
Asked about the Abu Dhabi talks, Merz said it was “important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement”.
“I do not see that happening so far,” the chancellor said.
Zelenskyy’s visit to Berlin was not announced in advance for security reasons.
On landing, he said on X that diplomatic coordination, strengthening air defences and supporting Ukraine’s energy sector would top the agenda.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US on Monday. He said the discussions would focus on “post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace”.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that a Russian delegation would attend, led as before by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported.
Europe seeks a seat at the table
The build-up to next week’s talks follows one of the most notable displays of cooperation between the warring sides since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Last week, human rights ombudsmen from Russia and Ukraine oversaw a local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in a mission brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Putin and Zelenskyy have had no direct contact since the invasion, and their representatives have held only a handful of rounds of talks.
Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane, reporting from Berlin, said there was a clear sense from Zelenskyy and Merz that the Abu Dhabi meeting “is a step forward, and there was an element of positivity about it”.
He said one journalist raised an important issue, saying “Europe and Ukraine are supposedly in lockstep with each other”, before asking, “why then are the Europeans not going to be in Abu Dhabi in those talks?”
“There was not much of a reply there, but it’s clearly an issue, a thorny issue, perhaps, certainly for the Europeans,” Kane said.
European governments have insisted on being involved in the negotiations but are unlikely to be at the table in Abu Dhabi.
Instead, US envoys are due to meet representatives from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, NATO and the European Union in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe’s post-war security architecture.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs an additional 70 billion euros ($77.5bn) from European countries next year.
Kane said successive German governments had pledged their full support to Ukraine, financing its efforts to fend off Russian attacks and supplying weapons and ammunition.
But he said Merz knows that “the financial aspect of helping Ukraine has become a real issue, given that the economy here and in other European countries is particularly threatened right now”.
“The cost of living in this country for many voters has become a serious issue,” Kane said.
He added that parties opposed to funding Ukraine, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Die Linke, were “prospering in the polls and in elections”.
Several summits are planned before year-end
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin may hold three-way talks on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 18 and 19 .
Around the same time, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of about 35 countries backing Ukraine, is due to meet in Berlin.
The Group of 20 (G20) summit follows in Florida from December 13 to 15 , where it remains unclear whether Putin will attend for the first time since the invasion.

articles.title: Defense contractors to demo cargo drones for US Marine Corps
articles.snippet: An event early next year in Huntsville, Alabama, will allow contractors to display their solutions for a Marine battlefield cargo drone.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Marine Corps and Navy will be conducting a technology demonstration for a Marine battlefield cargo drone early next year.
The event, from Jan. 25 to Feb. 5, 2027, in Huntsville, Alabama, will allow contractors to display their drones for the Increment II the Marine Corps’ Tactical Resupply Unmanned Aircraft System, or TRUAS, program.
TRUAS Increment II aims to “provide an organic aerial distribution capability for small-unit logistics support across the last tactical mile in expeditionary advanced base operations and distributed operations,” according to the Monday announcement by the Navy’s Air Warfare Program Management Office, which is sponsoring the demonstration.
Contractors will perform up to five flights, as well as demonstrate ground setup and flight preparation.
The first flight calls for a drone to transport a 100-pound payload up to 40 nautical miles under no-wind conditions, drop off the cargo either automatically or under manual control, and then return to the launch site without refueling. The second flight involves carrying and depositing a payload of 150 pounds or more out to 10 nautical miles.
The UAV must have a speed of at least 50 knots per hour and fly no higher than 1,000 feet during the flights. The UAS must be capable of launch and recovery without mechanical equipment such as a catapult, arresting net or cable.
“Following the two required flights, participants may be given the opportunity to perform up to three additional flights to demonstrate unique features and/or capabilities,” the Navy said.
The announcement lists a variety of technical specifications. They include flying at an altitude of up to 4,500 feet and, eventually, 8,000 feet. Speed should be a minimum of 50 knots per hour, with an eventual goal of 150 knots per hour, in crosswinds of 20 to 30 knots.
The Marine Corps is looking for an unmanned aircraft that can function autonomously, such as assessing the landing zone “before and during landing, day and night, and detect and avoid personnel, equipment, structures, excessive slope, and other terrain hazards.”
With skies becoming saturated by drones, TRUAS craft should have safeguards against collisions, including an “organic airborne sense-and-avoid capability for manned and unmanned aircraft at cruise speed, with performance comparable to a human pilot operating under Visual Flight Rules and sufficient reaction time for collision avoidance.”
The service also anticipates that its cargo drones will be forced to land under enemy fire.
“TRUAS shall minimize the time required to descend from cruise altitude to the LZ [landing zone] to enhance survivability by reducing the window for hostile detection,” the announcement noted.
The announcement did not specify what kind of cargo TRUAS will carry.
Last month, Ukraine claimed to have performed the world’s first drone medevac of a casualty from a frontline position. Ukraine’s 92nd Separate Assault Brigade posted a dramatic video of a wounded soldier being hoisted on a sling attached to the underside of a large hexacopter.
“Heavy Russian drone activity and mined terrain made evacuation by an unmanned ground vehicle impossible,” said Ukrainian media. “Working with the manufacturer, the troops developed a technical solution that allowed the heavy drone to carry the wounded soldier while remaining stable in flight, preventing it from tipping over or swaying excessively.”

articles.title: On American destroyers, avoid a self-inflicted wound in Spain
articles.snippet: "The Trump administration should keep six destroyers stationed at Rota. Any other action would be a gift to America’s adversaries."
articles.full_text:
Sometimes friends behave badly. When that happens, it is not smart to hurt yourself in retaliation for the friend’s bad behavior. That is true in one’s personal life — and also when it comes to defense strategy.
Consider the case of the Trump administration’s ongoing review of U.S. force posture in Europe and whether Washington will maintain a handful of American naval destroyers forward-stationed in Rota, Spain. Stationing destroyers at Rota helps secure vital American interests in Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East and allows the ships to spend more time conducting missions than traversing back and forth across the Atlantic.
To be clear, the government in Spain has certainly not been working overtime to win favor in Washington. Madrid has stubbornly refused to honor its NATO defense spending commitments, spending a paltry 2% of the country’s gross domestic product on defense. “2.1%, no more, no less,” President Pedro Sanchez said in June. “We fully respect the legitimate desire of other countries to increase their defense investment, but we are not going to do it,” he said.
To make matters worse, earlier this year, Madrid also restricted the U.S. use of Spanish airspace or military bases for operations against Iran.
With the administration openly weighing significant troop reductions across the continent, Spain’s actions may have put it near the top of the candidate list for cuts. But a careful examination makes clear that removing the destroyers based at Rota or closing the base there would be a big mistake.
The base hosts six Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers, up from four under a 2023 agreement. These vessels, which pack a powerful punch, can conduct anti-air, anti-submarine, and anti-surface warfare missions. The ships’ Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense upgrade enables them to defend against ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones. There is no other platform that combines mobile, multi-mission air and missile defense with the endurance to stay on station for months at a time.
Those capabilities have proved pivotal in recent conflicts in the Middle East. Over the past two years, Rota-based destroyers have rotated continuously into the Eastern Mediterranean. As many as four have been on station in those waters, simultaneously defending American interests and supporting the defense of Israel against Iranian ballistic missile attacks. That has saved the lives of Americans and Israelis.
The same ships also provide NATO’s sea-based missile shield against threats from the Middle East. That shield is important to protecting American bases in Europe and their ability to project power into the Middle East and North Africa. The destroyers also serve as the Navy’s forward presence for countering Russian submarine and surface activity in the Mediterranean and increasingly assertive Chinese naval activity off the African coast.
Some might ask whether these vessels can be replaced with European vessels. The answer is no, at least in the short term.
Years of under-resourcing have left European navies a mess. Spain’s own Álvaro de Bazán-class frigates are the most capable European warships, but Europe’s collective sea-based ballistic missile defense capacity remains thin to non-existent, and no European navy can surge Aegis BMD-equivalent coverage into the Eastern Mediterranean the way U.S. destroyers from Rota can.
If Washington brings the American destroyers home to the continental United States, the gap in missile defense coverage for NATO’s southern flank, Israel, and shipping lanes vital to the American economy would not be filled by European navies anytime soon and could potentially create a dangerous security gap for years or even decades.
Plus, a destroyer homeported in Spain, as part of Forward Deployed Naval Force-Europe, spends dramatically more time on station and far less time in transit than a U.S.-based ship that must cross the Atlantic to reach the same waters. That multiplies the combat power each hull generates over its service life.
If anyone in Washington doubts these arguments, consider the current actions of the Pentagon. It has increased the number of destroyers at Rota from four to six, with the final ship arriving only this year. In a recent interview, U.S. 6th Fleet Commander Vice Adm. Jeffrey Anderson suggested the sixth destroyer could not arrive soon enough. Clearly, senior U.S. military leaders believe we need more naval capacity stationed at Rota — not less.
Rota’s submarine support infrastructure, logistics hub, naval special operations support, and air operations also make it one of the most versatile forward installations the U.S. maintains anywhere, facilitating operations across Europe, the High North, Africa, and the Middle East simultaneously from a single location.
None of this means the diplomatic friction with Madrid should be ignored. Washington has every right to press Spain on burden-sharing, defense spending, and foreign policy differences. Washington may need to impose some consequences for Madrid’s decisions, but those should not include self-inflicted wounds that hurt U.S. military readiness and power projection capabilities, making Americans less safe.
The Trump administration should keep six destroyers stationed at Rota. Any other action would be a gift to America’s adversaries.
Rear Adm. (Ret.) Mark Montgomery and Bradley Bowman are senior directors at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. Montgomery served 32 years in the U.S. Navy, including as deputy director for plans, policy, and strategy (J5) at U.S. European Command. Bowman served in the U.S. Army as a Black Hawk pilot, taught at West Point, and advised members of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees.

articles.title: French defense minister kicks off ‘pact’ with industry in rush to field naval drones
articles.snippet: The French government is kicking off a new “pact” with the defense industry aimed at fostering a national ecosystem of drone makers that can quickly make new equipment tailored to its navy’s requirements.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — The French government is kicking off a new “pact” with the defense industry aimed at fostering a national ecosystem of drone makers that can quickly make new equipment tailored to its navy’s requirements.
Minister of the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin announced the initiative on Nov. 3, the first day of the Euronaval defense trade show, describing it as a novel mechanism for “converging” the needs of the armed forces.
The plan is akin to what French officials have been doing in the race to field new aerial drones, a technology that has become a fixture so central to modern combat that militaries worldwide are reorganizing to incorporate unmanned platforms.
In a statement, the French defense ministry highlighted some of the technology areas that could benefit from the new government-industry framework aimed at naval drones. For example, unmanned platforms will play a role in removing sea mines, collecting hydrographic and oceanographic data and exploring the ocean floor at great depths.
“Mastering” the seabed, as the original French wording goes, has been a fixture in the country’s naval-technology strategy for some years. The makeup of much of the seabed worldwide remains a blind spot for governments, just as critical infrastructure installed there — data cables and pipelines — has become a target for sabotage and outright warfare in the extreme underwater domain.
To that end, one agenda item announced at the trade show by French defense officials related to the naval drone framework is the purchase of a second ROV Deep Sea drone from LD Travocean, which, weighing 3,600 kilograms, can dive to 6,000 meters. The first ROV, ordered in 2024, completed qualification trials for its intended depth last week.
Related announcements include the planned acquisition of eight A18 countermine robots from Exail, a multi-sensor underwater drone for finding and characterizing sea mines before their eventual removal.
The French Navy will also buy a second unmanned combat underwater vehicle from Naval Group — this one a “bit longer” than the first test vehicle, coming in at over 10 meters in length and weighing in at more than 10,000 kilograms, a ministry spokesman told Defense News. The massive drone is meant to stay in the water for weeks at a time.
Defense officials also signed a deal with Naval Group and MBDA here to equip France’s FDI frigates with more Aster interceptor missiles. That entails retrofitting the onboard firing capability from 16 missiles to 32 on existing frigates, and ensuring new ones are built with the 32-launch-cell magazine baked in.

articles.title: On ‘NATO’s lake,’ Nordic allies worry about escalation with Russia
articles.snippet: Sweden, Finland, and their allies now face a challenge in countering Russian behavior without stoking tensions further.
articles.full_text:
When Sweden and Finland applied to join NATO in May 2022, it was hailed as the Baltic Sea’s transformation into “a NATO lake.” Since then, however, the sea has been less than placid, as confrontations with Russia and interference with undersea infrastructure have raised tensions to new heights.
Sweden, Finland, and their allies now face a challenge in countering Russian behavior without stoking tensions further.
“It’s a very difficult question, because you don’t want to escalate,” Maj. Gen. Peter Boysen, chief of the Danish army, said at the Association of the U.S. Army annual conference in Washington, D.C., in mid-October.
The Baltic has long been a site for hybrid warfare — a broad term for malign activity below the threshold of war that is often hard to attribute, like disinformation, sabotage, cyberattacks and territorial violations — but the scale of that activity has increased since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, creating what Dutch military intelligence earlier this year called “a real risk of unintended and therefore difficult-to-control escalation.”
One of the highest-profile cases was the Nord Stream pipeline attack in September 2022. Since then, other pipelines and cables in the Baltic have been damaged in what Western officials often label acts of sabotage. Alongside frequent GPS jamming, NATO allies are also seeing more airspace violations by Russian aircraft and more drone incursions at sensitive sites, like military bases and airports.
Russia consistently denies responsibility for those acts, but NATO leaders link them to Moscow’s efforts to undermine its neighbors, partly in retaliation for their support of Ukraine, and they have been more vocal in calling those efforts out.
In an assessment published in September, Denmark’s Defense Intelligence Service said “Russia has intensified its use of sabotage, destructive cyber attacks and is attacking targets in Europe with drones.” It added: “The hybrid war is escalating.”
Russia has also been more actively protecting “shadow fleet” vessels it uses to skirt sanctions, including by sending warships to escort them through the Baltic. That has led to confrontations with NATO.
“Russian forces are increasingly acting aggressively towards NATO military units in the Baltic Sea region,” the assessment said.
“The most recent and most serious example,” the assessment cites, was an incident on Sept. 14 in which a Russian frigate near Denmark’s coast fired flares at a Danish military helicopter.
That incident epitomized the challenge of deterring such behavior, Boysen said during a panel event at the conference. “How should your response be to that? It would, for us, be to de-escalate, but we’ve also seen that when the pattern of our adversary’s operations change when they pass through the Baltic Sea, how do you respond to that in a balanced way so you’re not increasing [tensions] but you actually say, ‘We know this is not the right way to do it. We want to decrease it back to normal’?”
“What we don’t want to do is to move ‘normal’ to a new intensity level,” Boysen added. “Normal needs to be decreased, and that’s a very, very difficult question.”
Russia’s wartime footing and wariness of Ukraine’s long-range strikes also make “escalation control” difficult, Lt. Gen. Kari Nisula, the Finnish Defense Forces’ deputy chief of staff for operations, said during the panel.
When Russian forces operate in the Baltic, “they try to defend themselves [with] air-defense measures, force-protection measures, and I think they are kind of afraid that a missile will hit their ships and that kind of thing, which is quite normal,” Nisula said. “It’s a very difficult environment from an escalation-de-escalation perspective.”
While tensions around the Baltic Sea are not new, growing concern about hybrid threats has led NATO to increase its vigilance and cooperation there.
In October 2024, Germany set up Commander Task Force Baltic, a multinational command to coordinate naval activity and provide up-to-date maritime situational awareness to allies. Around that time, NATO’s Allied Command Transformation set up Task Force X-Baltic to accelerate employment of uncrewed systems and AI integration to better protect undersea infrastructure. In January 2025, NATO began Baltic Sentry, an open-ended operation to enhance the alliance’s presence and responsiveness in the region.
Nordic countries, Sweden and Finland in particular, are also collaborating to better monitor and defend their territory. This summer, in response to a spate of drone incursions in Finland and other NATO states, Stockholm authorized its military to help Helsinki maintain “territorial surveillance and territorial integrity,” Maj. Gen. Johan Pekkari, commander of the Swedish army, said during the panel.
“To use the air force as an example, we leave air assets to the air operational command of Finland, and they lead their sorties and [take] care of those drones,” Pekkari said. Sweden could eventually lend counter-drone systems to that effort as well, Pekkari said. “That is one example of how we cooperate when it comes to that kind of challenge.”
Boysen said that alongside “being able to project power,” the ability to detect and identify malign activity is necessary to counter Russian activity without sparking escalation.
“Being able to put light on the adversary, to tell the adversary we know what you are doing — I think that is the way to de-escalate it,” Boysen said. “If you don’t do anything and if you are not able to detect, I think you put yourself in a very bad situation, and that would change ‘normal’ and make it a new normal, which is in effect an increase, I think, in the threat to you.”
Some in NATO argue that highlighting the threat from Russia may only boost the Kremlin’s efforts to sow fear within the alliance and erode support for Ukraine. Others in the alliance say that transparency is necessary to keep their publics engaged and to maintain support for efforts to counter Moscow. Despite that debate, few NATO officials, especially those from frontline countries, expect Russia to change course.
“When it comes to Putin and his plans, there were hybrid attacks between 2014 to 2022. There were an increasing number of hybrid attacks after 2022, and I do think that I’m echoing how my colleagues are talking in Finland when I say that we might have to expect even more hybrid attacks in the near future,” Leena-Kaisa Mikkola, Finland’s ambassador to the U.S., said at an event hosted by the Atlantic Council and the Norwegian Embassy in Washington, D.C., in September. “I quote what our defense minister said a couple of days ago: the situation in the Baltic Sea is ‘quite lively.’”

articles.title: India orders next-gen corvettes for $5.7b under broad naval modernization push
articles.snippet: New Delhi is spending big money on new corvettes from domestic shipbuilders, carrier-capable fighters from France and submarines from Germany.
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI — In a major push to strengthen its naval capabilities, India signed a $5.7 billion contract with domestic companies Monday to build eight next-generation, corvettes that will undertake anti-submarine, anti-surface and coastal defense operations.
The new ships will gradually replace a fleet of aging single-role corvettes.
India’s efforts to upgrade its maritime strength include plans to acquire six advanced submarines through a partnership with Germany and base 26 French Rafale Marine aircraft aboard its aircraft carriers.
The Defense Ministry said the corvettes will be equipped with state-of-the-art capabilities, including advanced missiles, weapons and sensor suites enabling them to undertake missions across the air, surface and sub-surface domains.
The ministry said the project marks a “significant milestone in India’s indigenous warship design and construction capabilities” because it is the first project in which the ships will be designed by the Indian Navy and built in domestic, state-owned shipyards.
Designed as high-speed, stealth combatants, five of the corvettes will be built by Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers (GRSE) and three by Goa Shipyard. The vessels would have a length of 127 meters, a beam of 17.6 meters, a deadweight tonnage of 4,950 and a maximum speed of 26 knots, according to GRSE.
The corvettes will carry medium-range anti-ship, medium-range surface-to-air missiles and 324 mm torpedo tubes.
The induction of these ships will enhance the Indian Navy’s operational capabilities in safeguarding maritime trade routes, conducting anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare operations, strengthening coastal defense, and undertaking littoral combat operations according to the Defense Ministry.
With about 90% of India’s trade moving through maritime routes and a coastline stretching more than 11,000 km, protecting sea lanes and coastal waters is an important security priority for the country.
The corvettes are part of a wider push by India to bolster its naval strength amid China’s expanding presence in the Indo-Pacific and Pakistan’s deepening military cooperation with Beijing.
Chief of the Naval Staff, Admiral Dinesh Tripathi, said in February that India aims to become a navy with 200-plus ships by 2035. The navy currently has 145 ships and submarines.
That expansion includes plans to acquire six advanced submarines under an approximately $8 billion deal with Germany.
The German ambassador to New Delhi, Jasper Wieck, said in September that the proposed deal to build six next-generation conventional submarines has been set on the German side. “In terms of the documents, it has already been finalized and the German side has agreed to it. It is now up to the Indian side to complete and conclude its internal processes,” Wieck told reporters.
The proposed program involves German shipyard TKMS collaborating with Indian state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Ltd. to build the vessels in India. The submarines will be equipped with air-independent propulsion (AIP) technology, allowing them to remain underwater for longer periods than conventional diesel-electric submarines and making them particularly suited to patrols in the strategic waters of the Indo-Pacific.
Meanwhile, on Oct. 29, a Rafale Marine fighter jet also landed for the first time on India’s newest aircraft carrier INS Vikrant, marking a successful carrier compatibility trial.
The trial comes 18 months after India signed an approximately $7.5 billion contract with France to acquire 26 Rafale Marine aircraft, comprising 22 fighters and four trainer aircraft.
“The ongoing trials mark the first steps towards operationalization of the aircraft in the Indian Navy,” the Indian Navy said.
The Rafales already operate from French aircraft carriers, but their compatibility with the Indian ship’s different launch and recovery arrangements needs to be tested.
The French Rafales will join the Navy’s existing Russian MiG-29Ks and bring modern multirole strike capability to both of its carriers.

articles.title: Australia preps Bluebottle USV for submarine-hunting role
articles.snippet: "I want potential adversaries to understand that, when they see an Ocius Bluebottle USV, it’s a signal to get out of our ocean,” Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy said.
articles.full_text:
CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — Australia’s Navy is doubling down on unmanned systems as it adopts platforms like the Bluebottle unmanned surface vessel and Ghost Shark and Speartooth extra-large autonomous underwater vehicles.
The Bluebottle unmanned surface vessel – or USV for short – produced by Ocius Technology, is powered primarily by wind, wave and sun to give persistent, at-sea surveillance for weeks at a time.
“I’ve said before that I want potential adversaries to understand that, when they see an Ocius Bluebottle USV, it’s a signal to get out of our ocean,” Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy has said.
Australia possesses the world’s third-largest exclusive economic zone, behind only those of France and the United States.
As well as conducting surveillance, the autonomous Bluebottle has been given a new tool to help it hunt enemy submarines on Australia’s periphery: the BlueSentry thin-line, fiber-optic sonar towed behind the Bluebottle.
In fact, Thales Australia opened an assembly line for the BlueSentry sonar in late October 2026. This multimillion-dollar facility – jointly funded by the company and the Australian government – is located in western Sydney.
As well as the BlueSentry, the complex will design, make, integrate and sustain towed-array sonars for submarines and warships. Thales will produce towed-array sonars for Australia’s six incoming Hunter-class frigates being constructed by BAE Systems Australia.
Furthermore, the plant will sustain existing Thales sonars on Australia’s six Collins-class diesel-electric submarines.
“The new facility boosts this Australian-made deterrence by ensuring end-to-end sovereign manufacturing capability and capacity for next-generation, towed-array sonar systems that support submarines and surface combatants, and thin-line towed arrays for uncrewed maritime systems serving both Australian and export markets,” Thales Australia said in a statement.
Under Project Sea 1200, the Royal Australian Navy ordered 40 Bluebottle USVs for A$176 million (US$124 million) in March this year, while the country’s Border Command already operates 15 other Bluebottles to monitor waters north of Australia.
With demand for Bluebottles expanding, Ocius opened a new engineering, production and maintenance hub for the USVs in Sydney on Oct. 16, 2026. It incorporates a 24/7 global operations center to monitor Bluebottles crisscrossing the world’s oceans.
A week earlier, Ocius Technology opened its first maintenance base outside Australia. That facility is located in Auckland, New Zealand, and it will service two Bluebottles acquired by New Zealand’s navy in April 2025.
Last month, Australia also announced it was donating Bluebottles to Fiji. The first units should arrive there in early 2027, and they will help combat drug smuggling, illegal fishing and organized crime.
Australian Navy Chief Vice Adm. Matt Buckley said: “In terms of our platforms themselves, of course they must continue to evolve, and the evolution of modular payloads that we can fit to uncrewed vessels like the Ghost Shark, like the Speartooth, like the Bluebottle creates enormous flexibility for us and allows us to adapt these systems to future missions and future requirements.”

articles.title: Russia is giving its drones bigger antennas to beat Ukrainian jamming
articles.snippet: Kyiv now needs roughly twice as many jammers to stop each upgraded Shahed, intel officials and experts said.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is fitting drones with larger jam-resistant antennas, making it harder for Ukrainian forces to use electronic countermeasures to scramble their navigation signals, Ukrainian officials said.
Russia’s Kometa navigation modules, produced by the company VNIIR-Progress, use arrays of small receiving elements called patch antennas to keep satellite navigation working through jamming. They have been found on Geran drones, glide-bomb kits, Iskander-M and Kinzhal missiles and the new Filin cruise missile, according to a database of Russian weapons run by Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR.
The Kremlin is already using Kometa modules with 16-element antenna arrays at scale and is setting up serial production of 20-element arrays, increasing its capability to work out which direction jamming comes from and compensate for it, HUR said Oct. 19.
Shaheds carrying antennas with 32 elements have already been found attacking Kyiv, said Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an electronic-warfare specialist and adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology.
“The more elements, the more electronic-warfare signal sources the antenna can suppress,” he said in an October post on Telegram.
The larger antennas give Russia an asymmetric advantage by being easier to counter than to install, Beskrestnov said.
“This race is difficult for us because it is easier for the enemy to increase the number of elements on an antenna than it is for us to add electronic warfare sites,” Beskrestnov said.
Russia’s better-protected drones can fly through Ukraine’s EW shield — one of its most affordable and widespread layers of air defense — leaving more of them to be shot down by costlier options, like interceptor drones, jets and missiles.
A Kometa module’s resistance to jamming depends on the number and arrangement of its patch antennas, the receiving elements on the array, and on the algorithm its processing chip uses to separate the satellite signal from interference, HUR said.
Drones carrying the upgraded antennas can still be taken out by jamming more satellite bands at once or by networking devices to feed drones false coordinates, defense leaders say.
The commander of Ukraine’s Night Watch unit, who goes by the call sign Alkhimik, bought a 32-element antenna taken from a Shahed, “that had crashed and was being sold on the secondary market,” he told Militarnyi in July.
He discovered that the device was simply two 16-element arrays covering different satellite-navigation bands put together, he said, giving him inspiration on how to counter it.
“By creating two systems — one operating in the L1 band and the other covering L2/L5 — we’ll be able to jam this antenna without any problems,” Alkhimik said.
Spoofing works, too, according to Fly Group Ukraine. It links multiple devices into a network to feed a drone false coordinates, Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi, the defense company’s director of development, told Reuters in September.
“The drone continues to think it is flying toward its target, but its own autopilot, relying on the false coordinates, gradually changes course on its own and steers the craft away from cities into safe areas,” he said.
Russian defense firms have ordered more than 100,000 Kometa modules in various configurations this year to guide cruise and ballistic missiles, strike drones and guided bombs, HUR said, a measure of demand for the technology.

articles.title: US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
articles.snippet: The missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. State Department said on Friday it had approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, in what would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second Trump administration.
Delayed missile deliveries have added to Ukraine’s tensions with the U.S. after President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy for Ukraine’s unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country. The Patriot missile system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.
On Thursday, a Russian drone strike killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
Zelenskiy said on Monday that Ukraine had been waiting for almost a month for the U.S. to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure.
But despite Ukraine’s urgency, it will likely not receive the missile interceptors quickly. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfill, and two people briefed on the U.S. decision said the missiles — which are yet to be manufactured — are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.
One of the people said Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense is encouraging the Pentagon to bring forward the delivery date, possibly by giving Kyiv missiles already in the U.S. arsenal and backfilling with the new Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway routed through a program called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in a statement.
The program uses donations from allies to buy weapons, services and training for Ukraine to support its self-defense following Russia’s invasion, according to a Pentagon website.
The JUMPSTART program was used in August to buy 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.
Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale of the Patriot interceptors.
The U.S. has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defense and precision-guided weapons.
In July, the U.S. Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.
Lockheed has said that deal would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 MSE production capacity by the end of 2030 and increase jobs at its Camden, Arkansas, plant by 50%, to about 1,850 from 1,200. Lockheed previously announced Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would go to 2,000 units annually.
Pentagon negotiators are pressing contractors to move much faster, with tentative production agreements struck earlier this year at the center of efforts to increase missile output.

articles.title: BAE Systems launches new Sea Tridon naval gun series
articles.snippet: These variants are designed to adapt to newer, unmanned threats, and also feature some new technology upgrades.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — BAE Systems debuted a new series of naval guns designed to tackle airborne, surface, and shore threats today at the Euronaval defense show in Paris.
The family of guns is derived from the Bofors 40 Mk4 naval gun that first started development more than 15 years ago. Each of the three variants come with their own characteristics, all designed around trying to meet the needs of modern navies, according to the firm.
“The maritime threat landscape is evolving rapidly, creating a growing need for flexible and effective protection solutions,” Lena Gillström, president of BAE Systems Bofors, said in a news release Tuesday. “With the Sea Tridon, navies and maritime operators can select the capability level that best meets their operational needs while benefiting from a common platform, proven technology and advanced programmable ammunition.”
The three variants are:
- Sea Tridon, which combines the Bofors 40mm gun with an “integrated electro-optical fire-control system,” which the company says will make it easier to integrate onto new platforms.
- Sea TridonC, a containerized version of the Sea Tridon. Militaries around the world have been experimenting with containerized systems, which can be swiftly deployed and, if needed, abandoned after use.
- Sea Trinity, which the company claims is the “most advanced” of the family. It comes with the Bofars 40mm gun and integrated fire control radar, and is specifically to be used to counter the kind of small missiles and drones that have come to represent major threats to ships in the Black Sea and the Gulf.
Speaking to reporters at the show, Stefan Lofstrom, director of marketing and sales for BAE Systems Bofors, emphasized that the new systems will use the company’s already in production ammunition.
“Ammunition-wise, all those variants are compatible with our programmable 3P ammunition,” Lofstrom told reporters at Euronaval. “That’s been around on the market for a long time. It’s well proven again. That’s really the unique selling point with these systems: the 3P ammunition.”
Lofstrom said that conversations are also underway with “several navies” right now about the integration of the Sea Tridon guns on unmanned systems that would go out to sea without human support for weeks at a time, in order to work out how certain aspects, like gun maintenance and ammunition reloading, could be handled without crew aboard.
Customers for BAE’s Mk4 naval gun already include the Royal Navy and the Royal Netherlands Navy, who have purchased the weapon for some of their frigates. Additionally, others including the Royal Netherlands Navy and the Belgian Navy have selected the naval gun for their mine countermeasure vessels.
“The starting point for this family of new products is the existing customer base, but then we in parallel have ongoing customer conversations with I would say a handful or two handfuls of customers,” Lofstrom said. “We don’t have a launch customer for this yet, but we have some advanced discussions with different customers.”

articles.title: Syria weighs joining the Mecca Pact, foreign minister says
articles.snippet: “Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” Syria’s foreign minister Asaad al-Shaibani said.
articles.full_text:
BEIRUT — Months after the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Pact, Syria has expressed interest in joining, its foreign minister said.
“Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” Asaad al-Shaibani said during the IISS Manama Dialogue in Bahrain on Saturday.
The Mecca Pact, signed on Aug. 7, aims to “strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all. It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defense cooperation among the three states,” according to a joint statement by the three countries.
The three countries are expected to boost defense production cooperation with a trilateral ecosystem, experts told Breaking Defense in August. If Syria joins the alliance, it will be part of the defense production cooperation.
The Mecca Pact was signed amid increasing regional attacks from Iran-backed Houthis, and while Syria is recovering from a 14-year civil war that ended in December 2024.
Highlighting Syria’s stance amid the ongoing Iranian attacks on the Gulf states, al-Shaibani said that “Syria considers that the security of the GCC [Gulf Cooperation Council] and the Gulf is a part of its regional security and vice versa. Consequently, Syria stands by all the Gulf states. Regardless of any other political positions, we stand by the governments of the Gulf and the peoples of the Gulf to face all the challenges and all the trans-border militias.”
Al-Shaibani’s comments at the Manama Dialogue come as Syria eyes to end all foreign military bases in the country, according to a September speech by President Ahmad al-Sharaa. Al-Sharaa noted at the time that this move will allow the country to have “complete and pure sovereignty of the Syrian state.”
Similarly, al-Shaibani said at the Manama dialogue that Syria has “expelled militias that have intervened in Syria, and it is possible to convey this experience and to expand cooperation and collaboration with other countries facing the same problem. Because any weapon outside the scope of the state will weaken the state before harming the others and harming the neighborhood.”
Syria is not the only Arab state that might join the pact. Defense expert Riad Kahwaji told Breaking Defense in August that Qatar and Kuwait are other possible candidates.
“We already have a defense pact between Kuwait and Pakistan, and we have another one between Qatar and Turkey. So I believe these two countries would be the most likely first candidates to join this this pact,” Kahwaji said.

articles.title: Gambit Series offers a scalable path for collaborative combat aircraft
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Gambit represents a scalable solution designed to counter today’s threats and address tomorrow’s challenges.
articles.full_text:
The threats faced by crewed fighters on today’s battlefield have proliferated at a staggering pace. That’s why the time has come for the U.S., along with its allies in Europe and across the globe, to adopt autonomous Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) at scale.
The modern air defense environment has grown dramatically more lethal. Powerful radars, highly capable anti-air missiles, and loitering munitions now menace even the most advanced tactical aircraft. Ground-based, long-range missiles can threaten fixed targets, such as airfields, across entire regions.
These capabilities are no longer limited to major powers with advanced technology — they have trickled down to second-tier nations and even terrorist groups.
The reemergence of industrial-scale warfare demands an industrial-scale response. Yet the cost of still-vital crewed fighters has become unaffordable even to nations with world-leading defense budgets such as the United States.
Crewed-uncrewed teaming offers a solution. By using uncrewed fighters designed for simplicity and mass production, nations can affordably overwhelm, disperse, and eliminate enemy air defenses while diverting enemy tactical aircraft away from crewed fighters and bombers.
GA-ASI’s Gambit Series of Uncrewed Aerial Combat Vehicles (UCAVs) was developed to address precisely this challenge. Each Gambit is a mission-focused uncrewed combat aircraft designed to operate alongside crewed fighters.
A Modular Approach to Affordable Mass
Rather than building a single aircraft for every mission, GA-ASI created a modular family of uncrewed jet fighters with variants optimized for distinct operational roles.
This approach avoids the costs of multi-mission aircraft, which in many cases are not best suited for roles that require flying into the teeth of enemy air defenses. It also retains common hardware across the family. Indeed, Gambit strikes the right balance between cost and capability.
About 70 percent of Gambit’s key components, including the landing gear, baseline avionics, and core airframe structures, are shared among its variants. This commonality simplifies production, lowers lifecycle costs, and accelerates the creation of mission-specific aircraft.
The family includes:
- Gambit 1: Long-endurance ISR
- Gambit 2: Air-to-air combat
- Gambit 3: Adversary air training
- Gambit 4: Stealth combat reconnaissance
- Gambit 5: Carrier-based operations
- Gambit 6: Air-to-ground missions
Gambit 6 was developed specifically to meet the needs of European nations facing advanced, industrial-scale threats on their eastern front. It has been optimized for electronic warfare, suppression of enemy air defenses, and deep precision strike in contested environments.
Each Gambit features a signature-reducing internal weapons bay that supports the integration of electronic warfare systems, precision-guided munitions, sensors, and autonomy software.
The modular architecture and signature-reducing weapons bay allow for easy integration of advanced autonomy, sensors, and weapons systems, ensuring the aircraft can adapt to a wide range of operational scenarios.
Operational Experience and Production Readiness
The U.S. Air Force recently awarded an initial production contract to GA-ASI for its FQ-42 Vengeance Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA), a derivative of Gambit 2. This means that GA-ASI is already in serial production of the world’s first uncrewed fighter jet.
GA-ASI’s position in the CCA market is rooted in nearly two decades of development, both through independent research and development and in collaboration with the U.S. Air Force.
Leveraging its more than five million square feet of fully operational manufacturing facilities, GA-ASI is ready to begin producing aircraft at scale the moment a contract is awarded.
Optimized for European Requirements
For European customers, Gambit is a platform that supports sovereign integration and industrial participation.
General Atomics’ German affiliate, General Atomics AeroTec Systems GmbH, could support local assembly, integration, and testing for German programs, while partnerships with European industry would enable integration of national sensors, mission systems, and autonomy software.
GA-ASI expects Gambit 6 airframes to be available for international procurement beginning in 2027, with European missionized versions deliverable by 2029.
By choosing Gambit, European nations gain a combat-ready, sovereign platform that combines cutting-edge technology with domestic industrial growth and strategic autonomy.
With its unmatched capabilities, production readiness, and commitment to indigenous integration, Gambit represents a scalable solution designed to counter today’s threats and address tomorrow’s challenges.

articles.title: Former Army secretary Dan Driscoll heads to OpenAI
articles.snippet: “I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe,” Dan Driscoll said in OpenAI’s announcement.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Former Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll has joined OpenAI as a senior counselor for national security modernization — a newly established role — according to a release from the company and Driscoll’s LinkedIn page.
“National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years. This technology will help them keep pace by cutting through paperwork, making sense of more information, and getting the right answer to the right person faster,” Driscoll said in the company’s announcement Monday evening.
“I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe,” he continued.
In this role, the former 26th secretary of the Army will advise senior leadership and “external partners” on how AI can bolster national security and cybersecurity, with a specific focus on working with US allies to advance the “responsible use” of AI, per the company’s announcement.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he’s “excited to welcome Dan Driscoll to OpenAI to strengthen American leadership” and help the company work with other countries to “spread the adoption of democratic AI.”
Driscoll joins the company after the Pentagon’s high-profile fight with AI company Anthropic where the military wanted unrestricted access to Anthropic’s Claude model but the company ultimately refused. After months of back and forth, the altercation resulted in the Pentagon shifting its classified network integrations toward other AI providers including OpenAI.
Driscoll resigned from his secretary position in the Army in late August following months of a reported strained relationship with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. During his tenure as secretary, Driscoll, an Iraq War veteran who has a background in venture capital, prioritized military modernization with efforts such as Operation Jailbreak, the sprawling Army Transformation Initiative, the low-cost interceptor program and more.
According to his LinkedIn page, in between his stint as secretary and his new role at OpenAI, Driscoll served as an advisor at counter-drone company Perennial Autonomy and a public affairs firm Watchtower Strategy.
