articles.title: Sweden’s Saab launches family of AI agents for future aircraft projects
articles.snippet: Key to the autonomous project is Saab’s AI Fighter Jet Pilot Academy, designed to develop the agents and, in parallel, establish infrastructure necessary to “create, train and evaluate” them, says the firm.
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — Swedish manufacturer Saab has unveiled a suite of inhouse AI agents designed for future aircraft platforms, following testing of the new technologies on a Gripen E multirole fighter jet.
The move demonstrates the firm’s “ability to develop, train, and fly its own Al for air combat” operations, according to a company statement released today.
The company added that the agents use “various Al techniques to master tactical decision-making in complex operational environments.” They can also work with a pilot inside a cockpit or from its own uncrewed air vehicle.
Key to the autonomous project is Saab’s AI Fighter Jet Pilot Academy, designed to develop the agents and, in parallel, establish infrastructure necessary to “create, train and evaluate” them, noted the Saab statement.
“The harder question is how we turn this success [of flying with the agents] into a dependable capability that can learn, improve, and be relevant over time,” Peter Nilsson, head of Advanced Programs at Saab’s aeronautics unit, told Breaking Defense and other media ahead of the announcement. “[T]hat is the true purpose of the AI Fighter Pilot Academy.”
He stressed that the “strategic advantage” of producing AI-driven data, “increasingly comes from reducing the distance between experience, learning, and field-led capability.”
It is of “enormous value to have a software-driven fighter like Gripen who can cope with this [computer processing] speed,” added Nilsson.
To date, the AI agents have predominately been tested and integrated with the fighter jet under Beyond Visual Range (BVR) combat conditions, much like a similar flight test campaign from 2025, when Helsing’s Centaur AI tool was used to take control of the fighter jet and autonomously complete a number of BVR maneuvers.
Longer term however, Saab plans on leveraging the inhouse AI technology to advance development of its future air programs.
As Breaking Defense previously reported, the manufacturer is developing a trio of unmanned aircraft — the A1, A2 and A3 — on the path toward the design of a new loyal wingman drone.
The company’s latest foray into AI-based Gripen testing follows a handful of similar flight tests in 2025 when Helsing’s Centaur AI tool was used to take control of the fighter jet and autonomously complete a number of BVR maneuvers.
Meanwhile, in an effort to scale computer capacity for the AI agents, the firm has also decided to become partial founder in a Swedish government-backed initiative dubbed Sferical Al.
Nilsson said that without Sferical AI, “otherwise you have to go to Google or Amazon … and pay some money” meaning, “you maybe don’t have full control of your data.”
To retain such a capability in Sweden is “enormous” for Saab, he added, noting that the new initiative was formally inaugurated during a ceremony in Stockholm last month.
Per a Saab slide shared by Nilsson, Sferical Al is built using Nvidia’s DGX SuperPOD architecture that makes it possible to develop Large Language Model and Vision-Language Model capabilities to aid agent and operator communications.
When Sferical Al is applied to a one-hour simulated training flight, it can produce the equivalent of one billion flight hours for a human pilot. “The exponential [computational] curve is … really hard to comprehend,” explained Nilsson.

articles.title: Industry needs more consistent demand signal to scale UGV production: Autonomy consortium exec
articles.snippet: “I think [industry has] the challenge of understanding what the demand signal is, and then again where to put their dollars,” Warren Sponsler, the COO of NAMC, said in an interview.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army’s goal of scaling unmanned ground vehicles is being sabotaged by the service’s inability to provide clear, coherent demand signal to industry, according to an executive at the National Advanced Mobility Consortium (NAMC), a nonprofit organization bridging the Pentagon and industry for ground drone projects.
“I think [industry has] the challenge of understanding what the demand signal is, and then again where to put their dollars. We do talk a lot about these capabilities that the Army has asked for, but they [industry] want to know what’s next,” Warren Sponsler, NAMC’s COO, said in a recent interview.
“[Industry is] trying to align themselves to what’s next. I think that’s probably one of the biggest challenges — just being able to produce at scale.”
Oftentimes companies order parts and put stress on their supply chains before the Army has settled on a contract mechanism or specific capability, Sponsler said. The commitment from industry is there, but the commitment from the Army, or any service for that matter, is not distinct, Sponsler said, which can be rather discouraging for companies.
READ MORE: Is the Pentagon’s demand signal for drones working? It depends on who you ask.
“Following through on those programs, I think it is critical to maintain that relationship between government and industry,” Sponsler said.
Exercises also sometimes send a murky demand signal, Sponsler said. While the Army has invited industry to demonstrate ground autonomy platforms at several events, the sheer amount of opportunities and unclear mission objectives leave companies unsure where to invest their time and money.
“I think it’s kind of the opposite challenge in many cases,” Sponsler said when asked if he thinks there are enough Army exercises for industry to demo their platforms. “There are so many opportunities right now, and then companies, especially those small companies, are having to make often hard decisions as to which experiments they participate in, and which ones they choose not to.”
He added that “focusing some of the demonstration experimentation activities would be a help” to provide a clear demand signal.
“There’s a lot of opportunities right now that the Army talks about for robotics and autonomy companies to get their stuff out in the field, get user feedback, and I think what [industry] is looking for is, ‘What is that path to scaling? Like, where is that path to revenue?’
“The more that they can describe what capabilities they’re actually looking to field and put together, the better,” he said.
Programs Of Record
Sponsler said the Army’s venture capital acquisition hub, FUZE, has provided a strong example through its xTech competitions for how the service should focus its demonstrations on certain capabilities. For example, xTech has held demonstrations, which are a part of larger competitions that will result in contract awards, for autonomous logistics and sustainment projects and for autonomous breaching. The path to revenue is clear in such cases as companies know they could be the winner of an eventual contract.
Sponsler said he urges companies, especially the nontraditionals, to enter such competitions, but he also urges them pay close attention to the Army’s programs of record for ground autonomy as they are the most indicative of how the Army plans to spend its money. The challenge there: the Army’s programs of record for ground autonomy have also fallen prey to the same lack of clarity as its outreach to industry.
For example, within roughly 18 months, the Army altered its UxS program of record and transformed the former Robotic Combat Vehicle program into the Unmanned Ground Commercial Robotic Vehicle program but then dispersed that program into Project Sustainment and the Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability program.
The service also relocated its acquisition office for autonomy then stood up a separate Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy and redesignated its Futures and Concepts Command as the new Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM), which will work in coordination with the Pentagon’s newly established Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM).
The good news, Sponsler said, is that he believes the new AUTOWARCOM, which has yet to be formally established since it requires Congressional approval, and FASCOM will allow the Army and the Pentagon’s autonomy efforts to be better streamlined.
He said the new organizations will help in “providing additional focus to robotics and autonomy integration at the formation level, looking beyond a product and more to a capability,” Sponsler said.
“[It] should also help to align resources and leadership to best prioritize based on the services’ needs. As the Army operates in multiple domains — ground, air, sea — having a [DoD]-level organization with a vision across services should help to mitigate duplicative efforts and better align resources,” he added.

articles.title: British businesses caught in Europe-wide supermarket fridge attacks
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Supermarket and grocery store refrigerator controls across Europe were hacked in the early hours of Monday in the second such wave of attacks in recent weeks — following a first wave in France — with unidentified perpetrators defrosting fridges and causing stock to spoil.
articles.full_text:
British businesses caught in Europe-wide supermarket fridge attacks
Three meat suppliers in Britain are among businesses that have been caught in a wave of cyberattacks across Europe targeting refrigeration systems, according to an industry trade body.
Supermarket and grocery store refrigerator controls across Europe were hacked in the early hours of Monday in the second such wave of attacks in recent weeks — following a first wave in France — with unidentified perpetrators defrosting fridges and causing stock to spoil.
The Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told Recorded Future News that its three affected members were attacked through vulnerable Copeland XWEB supervisory controllers. Copeland did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
AIMS spokesperson Tony Goodger described the association’s members as “collateral” because they ran the same software. None of the affected members lost meat, he said, but the incident “must act as a reminder to all in the food industry, at whatever point in the supply chain they are, that their businesses may be seen by some as targets.”
No hackers have claimed responsibility for the attacks. British authorities say they have not attributed the incidents to any group, while a spokesperson for Belgium’s cybersecurity agency told Recorded Future News “it may never be possible to identify” who was behind them.
Langridge Organic, a British fruit and vegetable wholesaler, told trade publication The Grocer that it had also been attacked. The company’s managing director Alex Pearce said it "was amazing how many parameters" the attackers had changed after accessing the controllers.
Pearce said he was “pretty sure that I interrupted a live hacking event,” as he physically disconnected a fridge from the internet after observing it being remotely put into defrost mode. He said no stock was spoiled as a result of his team’s physical interventions.
All of the British suppliers were reportedly using vulnerable temperature controllers for which a firmware update had been available since August. According to a security note shared among AIMS members, firmware for Copeland XWEB — version 1.12.1 and earlier — contained “severe authentication bypass vulnerabilities that allow hackers to take control without a password.”
National impact ‘minimal’ says NCSC
Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said Tuesday it was aware of the refrigeration attacks and assisting affected organizations. Its staff had worked through the night in an attempt to proactively contact companies that it detected had vulnerable systems exposed to the internet.
Speaking at the launch of the agency’s annual report, Paul Chichester, its director of operations, said the impact was “minimal” so far.
Richard Horne, NCSC’s chief executive, added that “although at a national level the impact is minimal, if you’re running the business that’s been hit by that, it is an enormous issue for you and your employees and everyone else.”
The NCSC’s annual report raised the alarm about “the failure to implement even basic cyber protections” with Horne warning that Britain faced the “real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents” in the coming months.
The businesses impacted in the fridge attacks appear to fit that pattern, given that they were running firmware that was known to be flawed. In August, researchers at industrial cybersecurity company Claroty disclosed almost two dozen vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB Pro controllers.
In reference to the first wave of attacks in France, the NCSC said the attacks were not sophisticated. “This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time,” said Chichester.
Horne said the attacks on freezers were “really just sort of the foothills” of the threat the agency was warning of in its report. “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that, in some ways, you could say are waiting to be exploited,” he said.
Ollie Whitehouse, the agency’s chief technology officer, said he and his colleagues were “surprised to see some of these things being connected to the internet still in 2026, despite warnings that we have put out over the last couple of years.”
AIMS is urging the government to give the food sector a stronger place in Britain’s designation of critical national infrastructure. No individual food sector assets are currently designated as critical under existing legislation.
The sector is also not included under the forthcoming Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which would require the operators of essential services to maintain appropriate security measures — such as patching vulnerable systems promptly — or face a fine of up to £17 million ($22 million) or 4% of their global turnover for serious failures.
The European Union’s counterpart legislation, NIS2, also covers food production and distribution. However, as reported by Politico, its breadth has drawn criticisms for potentially also catching “ice cream makers, Christmas lights manufacturers and German landlords.”
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Binance CEO says ‘months-long campaign’ led to $6.3 billion theft as N. Korea denies responsibility
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: North Korean attackers "combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews," Binance said about the multibillion-dollar crypto heist it discovered in October.
articles.full_text:
Binance CEO says ‘months-long campaign’ led to $6.3 billion theft as N. Korea denies responsibility
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said North Korean hackers used a months-long attack involving multiple company employees to stage its headline-grabbing theft of $6.3 billion last week.
The company released a post-mortem on Tuesday morning, outlining a campaign that dates back to June and involved the compromise of multiple employee devices.
Binance CEO Richard Teng called it a “months-long campaign” that wasn’t the result of “one mistake or one breach.”
“Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign. It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” Binance said. “The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”
Investigators said the breach started in June, when an engineer downloaded malicious software to install a popular AI coding tool. Binance’s security team detected the malicious software and replaced the device but the hackers gained access to crucial information about the engineer and other people on the developer team.
The company noted that throughout 2026, it has caught and stopped 57 separate attempts by North Korean actors to breach the company, compromise employees or break into corporate systems.
These attempts involved fake job interview offers, malware disguised as developer tools, compromised browser extensions, malicious video conferencing tools and other social engineering campaigns.
Started with one device
By September, one of the campaigns was successful in compromising the device of a software engineer who was contacted for a fake job offer. During the second interview, the Binance employee was told to download an assignment that contained a malicious code repository.
That download kicked off the attack that led to the theft, giving the hackers access to Binance systems and the ability to replace legitimate tools with malicious ones.
The malware was not detected by Binance’s endpoint security protection tools, and the company said the attacker took further steps to conceal the malicious activity — removing traces of the initial compromise.
By October 20, the hackers began to move laterally, using their access to the compromised device of the engineer to gain control of two other devices. The attackers successfully got into critical cryptocurrency wallet tools by October 29 and used credentials stolen from the breached employees to trigger the initial attack.
Binance said the hackers used an internal wallet signing service to initiate the first transactions, which saw almost $400 million in various cryptocurrencies flow out of the platform.
The company was alerted to the large transfers and began an investigation, but then $1.4 billion in bitcoin left the platform. The hackers used other mechanisms to conduct 50 other transactions that enabled the theft of $6.34 billion.
Binance quickly coordinated with other platforms to freeze about $2.85 billion in assets and suspended withdrawals but could not stop millions more in funds from being stolen.
The company said it lost valuable time in stopping the attack because it had to develop specialized procedures in the moment to revoke access and authorizations.
“We have taken immediate action to contain the incident and strengthen the systems involved. The entry points identified as having been used in the attack have been closed,” Binance said. “Systems touched in the attack path have been rebuilt or replaced. We have also implemented tighter device controls, enhanced wallet-service risk controls and expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection.”
Binance said it has taken several other actions to enable quicker responses to security incidents. All of the compromised devices and wallets have been replaced, while the credentials used in the attack have been decommissioned.
It has also hired a security company to conduct a review of the incident to validate its findings and recommend additional actions.
The tactics described by Binance resemble dozens of other attacks North Korean hackers have conducted over the last five years.
Multiple cryptocurrency companies have reported laptops infected with malware as the source of breaches while Google and other cybersecurity firms have warned of North Korean campaigns using fake job interviews and exams as a way to gain entry to blockchain firms.
Earlier this year, alleged North Korean groups stole $290 million from the Drift crypto platform in another sophisticated operation involving fake companies, alleged actors and more.
North Korea denies role
Over the weekend, the FBI and other U.S. agencies blamed the theft on North Korea’s TraderTraitor — a state-sponsored group that has spent years perfecting lucrative attacks on cryptocurrency exchanges and platforms.
North Korean spokesperson Kim Yo Jong denied the country’s role in the attack on Monday, calling it an “absurd” effort to “damage the international image of the DPRK.”
“It is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace, the wealth common to mankind, and resolutely reject any attempt to politicize the cyber issue and use it as a means of interfering in the internal affairs with other countries,” Kim said.
The spokesperson eventually accused the U.S. of confiscating “illegally stolen cryptocurrency assets,” in an apparent reference to the Justice Department’s seizure of $15 billion worth of bitcoin from accounts allegedly linked to the chairman of a prominent Cambodian conglomerate who was indicted on charges that his company is behind a sprawling scamming empire.
Blockchain security firms like Elliptic said the hackers have used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains to conduct about 40,000 transactions while shuffling funds to a new wallet every 25 seconds.
Investigators from the United Nations and several other countries said North Korea has been responsible for stealing billions from cryptocurrency companies since 2017 — with much of the stolen money used to fund its sanctioned ballistic missile programs.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Russia dismantles infrastructure of VasyGrek cybercrime group, detains three suspects
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russia's Interior Ministry said Monday that police had dismantled the group's infrastructure and identified its suspected members following an investigation conducted with assistance from cybersecurity firm Kaspersky.
articles.full_text:
Russia dismantles infrastructure of VasyGrek cybercrime group, detains three suspects
Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a cybercriminal group known as VasyGrek in a rare public crackdown on a long-running Russian-speaking hacking operation.
The group, also known as Fluffy Wolf, has been active since at least 2016 and has primarily targeted Russian companies with phishing emails designed to steal credentials, gain access to corporate networks and deploy malware.
Russia's Interior Ministry said Monday that police had dismantled the group's infrastructure and identified its suspected members following an investigation conducted with assistance from cybersecurity firm Kaspersky.
The group's alleged leader has been placed under house arrest, while two suspected accomplices have been released under travel restrictions, according to ministry spokesperson Irina Volk.
Such arrests are unusual in Russia, where many well-known Russian-speaking hacking groups have operated for years despite being closely monitored by cybersecurity researchers and law enforcement agencies.
Volk said the group's activities had attracted the attention of law enforcement agencies in Russia, the United States and Europe, but did not elaborate on whether foreign authorities had assisted in the investigation.
The hackers relied on an extensive network of phishing websites impersonating financial and accounting services, as well as servers hosted abroad, authorities said. They also purchased remote administration tools on dark web marketplaces to gain covert access to victims' computers.
In one attack described by investigators, an employee in the accounting department of an unnamed company received an email in September 2025 that appeared to come from a business partner. The message contained a malicious attachment disguised as a routine financial document.
When the employee opened the file, the hackers allegedly gained remote access to the computer and the company's online banking system. They subsequently transferred more than 660,000 rubles ($8,000) to accounts under their control, according to the Interior Ministry.
Police searched the suspects' homes and offices, seizing computers, communications equipment and other evidence.
The crackdown came as VasyGrek appeared to be expanding its activities beyond Russia.
In research published Monday, Kaspersky said it had detected more than 100 attempted attacks attributed to the group between January and September 2026, targeting organizations in Russia, Belarus and Kazakhstan.
The hackers most frequently targeted metallurgical companies, wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial goods, and government agencies, according to the researchers. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance and agriculture sectors.
Kaspersky described VasyGrek as a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose operations relied heavily on targeted phishing and malware designed to provide remote access to corporate systems.
The suspects face charges related to theft and the creation or distribution of malicious software. If convicted, they could face up to 10 years in prison on the theft charge and up to five years on the malware charge.
The Interior Ministry said the group's hacking infrastructure had been dismantled, although it remains unclear whether the arrests will permanently end its operations
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Russia-linked cyber spies target Ukraine's war crimes investigations, military aid routes
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The hackers use relatively simple malware to steal sensitive documents, login credentials and other information from Ukrainian organizations, particularly those near the front line and the Russian border.
articles.full_text:
Russia-linked cyber spies target Ukraine's war crimes investigations, military aid routes
A previously unidentified Russia-aligned hacking group has been targeting Ukrainian government agencies, defense organizations and infrastructure used to transport foreign military aid, researchers have found.
The group, dubbed Gorbag, has been active since at least February 2025, according to a report published Tuesday by cybersecurity firm ESET. The hackers use relatively simple malware to steal sensitive documents, login credentials and other information from Ukrainian organizations, particularly those near the front line and the Russian border.
Unlike more sophisticated cyberespionage groups that seek to maintain access to compromised networks for months, Gorbag appears focused on stealing information quickly before removing traces of its malware, researchers said.
The group's targets closely align with Russia's wartime intelligence priorities, including monitoring Ukrainian war crimes investigations, assessing damage from Russian strikes and gathering information about military supplies and local defense activities.
About a quarter of the group's known targets are Ukrainian law enforcement and judicial institutions, according to ESET. Researchers said the attacks could be aimed at monitoring investigations into alleged Russian war crimes and efforts to identify Russian operatives and collaborators inside Ukraine.
Another quarter are local government bodies, mostly city councils in areas close to the front line. These institutions often collect information about damage caused by Russian airstrikes, including assessments of critical infrastructure and estimated repair times that are not publicly disclosed.
Access to such records could help Russian forces evaluate the effectiveness of their attacks, ESET said. The hackers may also be seeking information about local defense initiatives, including recruitment, military training and civil defense preparations.
Other targets include Ukrainian defense organizations and an entity identified by researchers as a major transportation hub for foreign military assistance. ESET did not name the facility but said it had previously been targeted by Russian airstrikes. The hackers could be seeking intelligence on incoming military supplies and the damage inflicted on transportation infrastructure, researchers said.
Gorbag's operations rely primarily on phishing emails containing malicious attachments, often disguised as official documents concerning administrative fines or taxes.
Once a victim opens an attachment, the hackers can steal saved browser passwords, cookies, VPN configurations and selected files, including Microsoft Office documents, email records and archives.
The group's main information-stealing tool, dubbed BeautyStealer, searches computers, removable storage devices and connected network drives for potentially valuable files. It then attempts to delete itself after transmitting the stolen information.
Gorbag also uses a tool called Prime ReverseShell, adapted from publicly available code, that allows attackers to remotely execute commands on compromised computers.
In early 2026, the hackers changed their methods to exploit a previously disclosed security vulnerability in WinRAR, a widely used file-archiving program. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-8088, allows attackers to execute malicious code when a victim opens a specially crafted archive. It was patched in July 2025 and had previously been exploited by RomCom, another Russia-aligned hacking group linked to cybercrime and espionage.
ESET said Gorbag's preference for quickly collecting information rather than maintaining persistent access could indicate that it works with other hacking groups, passing stolen credentials and documents to operators who carry out subsequent intrusions. Researchers have not established whether such cooperation is taking place.
"Despite its relatively unsophisticated toolset, the group demonstrates precise targeting and operational intent to contribute to Russia’s broader strategic goals in the war with Ukraine," ESET said. "As long as the war in Ukraine continues, we expect groups such as Gorbag to remain a persistent threat to Ukrainian governmental, justice, and defense entities."
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: UK faces ‘unprecedented rise’ in cyberattacks in coming months, warns cyber chief
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: "[V]ulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable," the NCSC's chief will warn in releasing the agency's annual report.
articles.full_text:
UK faces ‘unprecedented rise’ in cyberattacks in coming months, warns cyber chief
Britain faces the “real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents” in the coming months, the head of the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) will warn Tuesday.
Launching the agency’s annual report, NCSC Chief Executive Richard Horne will warn that the risk is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”
The warning follows an alert issued in June by the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which said AI would fundamentally transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. “The timeline is not years, it is months,” it said at the time.
Officials point to the surging levels of vulnerabilities being uncovered by vendors as evidence this transformation is underway. They warn the change is accelerating, even if experts have not yet observed a corresponding rise in exploitation.
“Major technology providers are now fixing hundreds of vulnerabilities in a single update … and the Linux kernel project alone patched more than a thousand vulnerabilities last month,” Horne will say, adding that AI “is enabling vulnerabilities to be found and fixed faster than ever.”
The risk from attackers deploying the technology remains significant. The NCSC will say it was “highly likely” that AI-powered malware would be used in a ransomware attack on Britain’s critical infrastructure by 2028, and warned that China and Russia will “routinely” be using AI in their cyber operations by that date.
The annual report stresses that AI “did not create these cybersecurity weaknesses,” but is instead exposing “years of technical debt and the failure to implement even basic cyber protections.”
The NCSC will say even hacks linked to state-sponsored actors were often conducted through internet-facing applications and by exploiting “vulnerabilities for which patches are available but have not been deployed in a sufficiently timely fashion.”
Speaking in the wake of the British government’s official budget, which revealed plans to consult on whether to hold technology companies liable for cyber breaches caused by insecure products, Horne will take aim at how existing business practices have led to the current status of widespread vulnerability.
“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap,” he will say, referencing organizations keeping end-of-life systems running as part of their operations and delaying upgrades for “cost efficiency” reasons.
He will warn that executives who fail to act will end up having to “look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain … when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”
The NCSC had called publicly for a “strategic policy agenda” last year, after efforts to address insecure technology had stalled. Its chief technology officer, Ollie Whitehouse, wrote last year that “the reality is that in 2025, we know how to build secure products and services” but “the business and commercial incentives to encourage adoption and sustainment of secure solutions are not sufficient.”
AI vs AI
The threat posed by AI can be countered, Horne will say, explaining how the British government — including NCSC, a part of the cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ — is planning to deploy it for security purposes.
“AI has the potential to be one of the greatest opportunities in cyber defence,” he is expected to say. The report reveals the government has already begun testing frontier AI systems to identify weaknesses in its own networks.
One such initiative, titled Project DROMOS, was initially planned to be a four-week pilot before being expanded into live government environments where it found “hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities.”
The agency plans next to look beyond government systems with a new £70 million ($93 million) NERV Centre — the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre. This is intended to use AI to build on some of NCSC’s existing projects to “identify vulnerabilities across our critical infrastructure and economy.”
A further £60 million ($80 million) has been allocated to the first phase of Cyber Shield, a national network of AI agents first previewed in July that Horne is expected to say “will embed cutting-edge agentic AI into machine speed cyber defence at a national scale.”
Under the plan, the NCSC will provide the platform and threat intelligence, while security companies and open-source developers will build AI agents to operate within organizations across the country. The initial phase will focus on detecting and blocking attacks, the report will say.
In the new report, the NCSC will say it believes the “structural advantage will remain with defenders” as AI transforms cybersecurity. It is defenders who “own or operate the environment, can instrument it, can change it and can define acceptable behaviour.”
“But,” it warned, “this advantage is not a given and realising it requires clear direction, investment and disciplined adoption.”
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

It’s comforting to know that they could ship 1.3 million smart TVs with malicious code and never know it. The consumer is lucky it was just botnets and not something much more personal and damaging.
> Google said today
[“I heard you got robbed.”](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Chris_Rock)
I would really appreciate a little less journalistic “neutrality” than I’m seeing these days. It’s not just you, Brian, but the larger spectrum of non-investigative news reports that just repeat what the talking heads say. A better framing to my thinking (and why I gave that Chris Rock excerpt from 1996) is that Google *enabled* this abuse and then sat on their hands as it grew and grew to well over a million devices! They are in no way the good guys here. The deeper story to be uncovered and disclosed is why have they only acted now?
> residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic
Which is why they all need to be blocked by firewalls. That includes the networks of ISPs who *host* the devices and do not act to end their customer’s abuse. None of them are network peers whose traffic should be routed; the record DDoS attacks would be over if the Internet were just managed around that one sane principle.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

If you’re on shared hosting, it’s worth opening a ticket and asking which PHP build they’re actually running instead of trusting the control panel: the version shown there isn’t always the one serving requests.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
